meta.title: Bright — AI emergency-scenario training
meta.description: An AI plays the patient or the doctor. You type what you'd actually do. Emergency-medicine roleplay drills for Android, free, built in the open by one developer.
meta.ogAlt: Bright — a step for your brighter future

hero.name: Bright
hero.tagline: A step for your brighter future.
hero.description: I'm building an AI training app for medical emergencies. The AI plays the patient — or the doctor — and you type what you'd actually do next.
hero.note: APK on GitHub Releases. There's no Play Store listing yet.

demo.label: Emergency session
demo.caption: An illustration of the interaction — not a recording of the app.

messages.text: It started twenty minutes ago. Feels like something heavy is sitting on me.
Vitals and a 12-lead ECG now. IV access, and chewable aspirin unless there's a contraindication.
BP 138/86, HR 102. The ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF.
Inferior STEMI. Activate the cath lab and get a right-sided ECG.

what.title: Roleplay, not flashcards
what.lede: Bright puts you inside an emergency and keeps it moving. The AI stays in character; you answer in your own words.

cards.title: The AI takes the role
cards.body: It plays a patient in an emergency — or a doctor putting questions to you. The situation unfolds as a conversation, not a list of options.

cards.title: You write the response
cards.body: Nothing to pick from. You type what you'd actually say or do next, the way you'd have to in the room.

cards.title: Nothing vanishes when you leave
cards.body: Exit a session whenever you want. It's kept in your history, so you can read the whole thing back later.

what.note: History is stored on your device only. Google sign-in and cloud sync are on the roadmap, not in the app yet.

steps.title: Open Bright
steps.body: The first launch is a short cinematic intro: the name resolves, a few tutorial pages, then a language pick — Korean or English, guessed from your phone and changeable in settings.

steps.title: Start a session
steps.body: You're dropped into an emergency scenario with the AI already in character.

steps.title: Answer in your own words
steps.body: Type your response and the scenario moves on from what you said. Voice input is planned; today it's typing.

steps.title: Review it later
steps.body: Leave whenever you like. Every past session sits in your history, waiting to be read back.

design.title: Quiet on purpose
design.lede: This is a tool for practising emergencies. It should feel competent and calm — never loud.

points.title: Monochrome, all the way down
points.body: White, black, and the grays between. No accent color competing for attention while you're trying to think.

points.title: Your phone decides light or dark
points.body: Bright follows the system setting instead of asking. So does this site — with a manual toggle if you disagree.

points.title: Motion that answers you
points.body: Every button and slider animates. Nothing bounces, nothing lingers. It's there so a tap feels acknowledged.

points.title: A first launch worth watching
points.body: Name reveal, tutorial pages, language selection. It takes a few seconds and sets the tone for everything after it.

status.title: Built in the open
status.lede: One developer, shipping in small versions. Here's exactly where things stand — including what isn't built yet.

items.name: Google sign-in and cloud sync
items.body: Your history is local to your device today. Signing in and syncing across devices is on the list.

get.title: Install it from GitHub

steps: Open the releases page on your Android phone.
Approve the install when Android asks — sideloaded apps need a one-time permission for your browser or file manager.
get.groqNote: The AI runs on Groq's free tier. Bright asks for a free Groq key the first time a session needs one — you can skip past it during setup. A page here to help you get and manage that key is planned.

footer.tagline: A step for your brighter future.

meta.title: Bright — frequently asked questions
meta.description: How Bright works, what it costs, where your history is stored, and what isn't built yet.

faq.title: Questions, answered plainly
faq.lede: If something here is out of date or missing, open an issue on GitHub — it's the fastest way to reach me.

items.a: Nothing. There's no paid tier, no subscription, no ads, and no in-app purchases. The AI runs on Groq's free tier using a key you provide.

items.q: Do I need a Groq API key?
items.a: Yes, for the AI to respond. Groq's free tier covers ordinary practice, and getting a key takes a minute on Groq's own console. Bright lets you skip the key during setup and only asks when a session actually needs it.

items.q: Is Bright on the Google Play Store?
items.a: No. A submission was attempted before, but store distribution isn't being pursued right now. The APK on GitHub Releases is the real way to install it.

items.q: Where is my session history stored?
items.a: On your device, in the app's own local database. It isn't uploaded anywhere, which also means it doesn't survive uninstalling the app or move to a new phone. Google sign-in and cloud sync are planned, not built.
No. The AI is a hosted service, so a session needs an internet connection. Your saved history stays readable offline.

items.q: Can I speak my answers instead of typing?
items.a: Voice input is planned, not shipped. Today a session is typed.
It's in active development, sharing the same core as the Android app through Kotlin Multiplatform. There's no build to install yet.
Korean and English. The first launch picks one based on your phone's language, and you can switch in settings at any time.

items.q: Which Android versions can run it?
Can I rely on what the AI says?
items.a: No. Bright is a practice tool, not a clinical reference. The AI invents scenarios and can be confidently wrong, so treat its scoring and feedback as drill material — never as guidance for a real patient.
The APK releases repo is public; the source repo is private for now. That may change, but nothing about the app depends on it.

items.q: How do I report a bug or ask for a feature?
items.a: Open an issue on the public releases repo on GitHub. It's a one-person project, so the honest answer on timing is: when I get to it.

meta.title: Bright — privacy
meta.description: What Bright stores on your device, what leaves it, and what is never collected. No accounts, no analytics, no ads.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lede: Bright has no accounts and no analytics. Almost everything stays on your phone. This page describes exactly what happens to what you type.

sections.heading: The short version
bullets: Your sessions and history are stored only on your device.
What you type during a session is sent to Groq, the AI provider, to generate the reply. Nothing else leaves your phone during a session.
The app checks GitHub for a newer release. That request contains no personal data.
There is no account, no analytics or crash-reporting library, no advertising, and no third-party tracking in the app.
I never receive your session content. There's no server of mine for it to go to.

sections.heading: What's stored on your device
paragraphs: Bright keeps a local database on the phone. It holds your practice sessions, the messages in them, and the per-question records used to build your history and score summaries.
bullets: Sessions, messages and question records — the drills you've done.
Your language choice, chosen AI model, and the flags that remember you've finished the intro.
Your Groq API key, stored in the app's own preference storage on the device.
A practice streak count and whether the app has already asked you about notifications.
sections.after: Uninstalling Bright removes all of it. Because none of it is backed up to a server, an uninstall is permanent — that's the trade-off of local-only storage.

sections.heading: What leaves your device
paragraphs: The app talks to exactly two hosts, and nothing else.
bullets: api.groq.com — during a session, your typed messages and the scenario context are sent to Groq using your own API key, so the AI can reply. Groq's handling of that data is covered by Groq's own privacy policy and the terms of the account your key belongs to.

api.github.com — the app reads the latest published release of the public tyngzfgsf/Bright-app repository to tell you when an update is available. This is an ordinary anonymous web request; it carries no session content and no identifier from the app.

sections.heading: What is never collected
bullets: No account, sign-in, email address or profile.
No analytics, telemetry, or crash-reporting SDK is bundled in the app.
No advertising, and no advertising identifier.
No contacts, no location, no photos, no files from your phone.
Nothing is sold or shared with data brokers, because nothing is collected in the first place.

sections.heading: Permissions the Android app asks for
bullets: Internet and network state — to reach the AI and to check for updates.
Notifications — for practice reminders scheduled on the device itself. There is no push service behind them.
Install packages — so the app can offer to install a newer release it downloaded from GitHub.
Microphone — declared for speech input. Where it's used, the request is handed to Android's own speech recognition rather than recorded by Bright, and no audio is stored by the app.

sections.heading: This website
bullets: No analytics, no tracking pixels, and no advertising cookies.
One cookie, NEXT_LOCALE, is written only if you press the KO/EN language switch, so your choice sticks. Automatic language detection never writes it.
Your light/dark preference is kept in your browser's local storage and never leaves the browser.
The hosting provider keeps ordinary server request logs, as any web host does.

sections.heading: Don't type real patient information
paragraphs: Bright is for practice on invented cases. Please don't enter real patients' details, identifiers, or records — that content would be sent to a third-party AI provider, and the app has no safeguards designed for handling real medical records.

sections.heading: Your control over your data
bullets: Delete individual sessions from your history inside the app.
Remove or replace your Groq API key in settings at any time.
Uninstalling the app deletes the local database and preferences along with it.

sections.heading: Children
paragraphs: Bright is aimed at people training in emergency medicine and isn't designed or directed at children.

sections.heading: Planned changes
paragraphs: Google sign-in and cloud sync are on the roadmap. Neither exists today, and neither is silently switched on: when they ship, they'll be an explicit choice in the app and this page will be rewritten before that release goes out.

sections.heading: Contact
paragraphs: Bright is made by one developer. Questions about privacy — or corrections to this page — are best raised as an issue on the public GitHub repository, which is also the fastest way to get an answer.

meta.title: Bright — terms of use
meta.description: The terms for using Bright, including the medical disclaimer: it is a training tool and not medical advice.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.lede: Plain terms for a free app made by one person. The important part is the first section: Bright is training, not medical advice.

sections.heading: Bright is not medical advice
paragraphs: Bright generates fictional emergency scenarios so you can practise responding to them. It is an educational tool. It is not a clinical decision-support system, not a reference, and not a substitute for training, supervision, protocols, or professional judgement.
Do not use Bright to make decisions about a real patient. In a real emergency, contact your local emergency service — 119 in Korea, 911 in the United States — or follow your institution's protocol.

sections.heading: The AI can be wrong
paragraphs: Responses, scenarios, scores and feedback are produced by a large language model. It can state incorrect things confidently, misjudge an answer, or invent details that don't reflect real clinical practice or your local guidelines. Treat everything it produces as drill material to be checked against real sources, not as an authority.

sections.heading: Using the app
bullets: Bright is free for personal training use.
Don't enter real patient information or anyone else's personal data into a session.
Don't use the app for anything unlawful, or in a way that breaks the terms of the AI provider whose key you're using.
You're responsible for keeping your own API key secure, and for any usage charges your provider account incurs.

sections.heading: Third-party services
paragraphs: The AI runs on Groq, using an API key that belongs to you. Your use of that service is governed by Groq's own terms and privacy policy, and Bright has no control over their availability, pricing, or model behaviour. Releases are distributed through GitHub, which has its own terms.

sections.heading: No warranty
paragraphs: Bright is provided as is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied — including fitness for a particular purpose. It's a free app built in someone's spare time; it may contain bugs, produce wrong output, lose locally-stored data, or stop working after a platform change.
To the fullest extent the law allows, the developer isn't liable for any loss or damage arising from using — or being unable to use — the app, including anything arising from relying on its output.

sections.heading: Availability and changes
paragraphs: Bright is in active development. Features can change or be removed, releases can be delayed, and the project could stop being maintained. Because releases are published as APKs on GitHub, a version you've already installed keeps working as long as your device supports it.

sections.heading: Ownership
paragraphs: The Bright app, its name, and its design belong to the developer. Downloading and using released builds is fine; redistributing modified copies as though they were Bright is not. Sessions you produce with the app are yours.

sections.heading: Governing law
paragraphs: These terms are governed by the laws of the Republic of Korea, where the developer is based, without regard to conflict-of-law rules.

sections.heading: Changes to these terms
paragraphs: If these terms change, the date at the top of this page changes with them. Continuing to use the app after that means the updated terms apply.

sections.heading: Contact
paragraphs: Questions about these terms can be raised as an issue on the public GitHub repository.
